paragraphs: Sir,

Having read with great pleasure the pamphlet on national education that you recently published, I dedicate this volume to you — the first dedication I have ever written — in order to induce you to read it attentively; and I do so because I think you will understand me, which I do not expect of the many impertinent little wits who may ridicule the arguments they cannot answer. But, sir, my respect for your understanding goes further still: so far that I am confident you will not toss my work aside and hastily conclude that I am wrong merely because you did not see the subject in the same light yourself. And forgive my frankness, but I must remark that you treated it too superficially, content to regard it as it had been regarded in the past, when the rights of man, to say nothing of woman, were trampled on as a fantasy. I therefore call on you now to weigh what I have put forward concerning the rights of woman and national education; and I call with the firm voice of humanity. For my arguments, sir, are dictated by a disinterested spirit: I plead for my sex, not for myself. I have long considered independence the great blessing of life, the basis of every virtue; and I will always secure my independence by reducing my needs, even if I had to live on a barren heath.

It is, then, affection for the whole human race that sends my pen darting swiftly across the page in support of what I believe to be the cause of virtue; and the same motive makes me earnestly wish to see woman placed in a position in which she would advance, rather than hold back, the progress of those glorious principles that give substance to morality. Indeed, my opinion on the rights and duties of woman seems to follow so naturally from these simple principles that I think it hardly possible that some of the broad minds who framed your admirable constitution will not agree with me.

In France there is undoubtedly a wider spread of knowledge than in any other part of Europe, and I attribute this largely to the social contact that has long existed between the sexes. It is true — I state my views freely — that in France the very essence of sensuality has been distilled to delight the pleasure-seeker, and a kind of sentimental lust has prevailed. Together with the system of duplicity taught by the whole character of their political and civil government, this has given the French character a sinister sort of shrewdness, properly called finesse, and a polish of manners that damages substance by driving sincerity out of society. And modesty, the fairest garment of virtue, has been more grossly insulted in France than even in England, until their women have come to treat as PRUDISH that attention to decency which animals observe by instinct.

Manners and morals are so closely related that they have often been confused; but although manners should be no more than the natural reflection of morals, when various causes have produced artificial and corrupt manners, which are picked up very early, morality becomes an empty word. The personal reserve and the sacred regard for cleanliness and delicacy in domestic life, which French women almost despise, are the graceful pillars of modesty. Yet far from despising them, if the pure flame of patriotism has reached their hearts, these women should work to improve the morals of their fellow citizens by teaching men not only to respect modesty in women but to acquire it themselves, as the only way to deserve women’s esteem.

In arguing for the rights of women, I build my main case on this simple principle: if woman is not prepared by education to become man’s companion, she will halt the progress of knowledge, for truth must be common to all, or it will have no effect on general practice. And how can woman be expected to co-operate unless she knows why she ought to be virtuous — unless freedom strengthens her reason until she understands her duty and sees how it is connected with her real good? If children are to be brought up to understand the true principle of patriotism, their mother must be a patriot; and the love of mankind, from which an orderly succession of virtues springs, can only be produced by considering the moral and civil interest of mankind. But woman’s present education and situation shut her out from such inquiries.

In this work I have put forward many arguments, which I found conclusive, to prove that the prevailing notion of a distinct sexual character undermines morality. I have argued that, to make the human body and mind more perfect, chastity must be more widely practised, and that chastity will never be respected among men until a woman’s person stops being, as it were, idolized when little virtue or good sense adorns it with the noble marks of mental beauty or the touching simplicity of affection.

Consider these observations calmly, sir, for a glimpse of this truth seemed to open before you when you remarked “that to see one half of the human race excluded by the other from all participation of government, was a political phenomenon that, according to abstract principles, it was impossible to explain.” If so, what does your constitution rest on? If the abstract rights of man can withstand discussion and explanation, then by the same reasoning those of woman will not shrink from the same test — although a different opinion prevails in this country, founded on the very argument you use to justify the oppression of woman: prescription, the authority of long custom.

Consider — I address you as a legislator — whether, when men fight for their own freedom and for the right to judge for themselves what makes them happy, it is not inconsistent and unjust to subjugate women, even though you firmly believe you are acting in the way best suited to promote their happiness? Who made man the sole judge, if woman shares with him the gift of reason?

Tyrants of every kind argue in this style, from the weak king to the weak father of a family; they are all eager to crush reason, yet always claim that they usurp its throne only in order to be useful. Do you not play a similar part when you FORCE all women, by denying them civil and political rights, to stay walled up in their families, groping in the dark? For surely, sir, you will not claim that a duty can be binding if it is not founded on reason? If this really is their destiny, arguments for it may be drawn from reason; and, with such dignified support, the more understanding women acquire, the more attached they will be to their duty, because they will comprehend it. For unless they comprehend it, unless their morals rest on the same unchanging principles as man’s, no authority can make them carry it out virtuously. They may be convenient slaves, but slavery will have its constant effect, degrading both the master and the abject dependent.

But if women are to be shut out, without a voice, from sharing in the natural rights of mankind, then prove first, to fend off the charge of injustice and inconsistency, that they lack reason. Otherwise this flaw in your NEW CONSTITUTION, the first constitution founded on reason, will always show that man must, in one form or another, act like a tyrant; and tyranny, wherever in society it raises its brazen face, will always undermine morality.

I have repeatedly asserted, and supported with what seemed to me unanswerable arguments drawn from matters of fact, that women cannot be confined by force to domestic concerns. For however ignorant they are, they will meddle in weightier affairs, neglecting their private duties only to disrupt, with cunning tricks, the orderly plans of reason that rise above their comprehension.

Moreover, as long as women are brought up to acquire nothing but personal accomplishments, men will look for pleasure in variety, and unfaithful husbands will make unfaithful wives. Indeed, such ignorant beings will be very excusable when, never taught to respect the public good nor granted any civil right, they try to obtain justice for themselves by retaliation.
Once this box of mischief has been opened in society, what is left to preserve private virtue, the only safeguard of public freedom and universal happiness?

Let there be, then, no coercion ESTABLISHED in society, and as the ordinary law of gravity takes effect, the sexes will settle into their proper places. And now that fairer laws are shaping your citizens, marriage may become more sacred; your young men may choose their wives out of affection, and your young women may let love uproot vanity.

The father of a family will then no longer weaken his health and debase his feelings by visiting prostitutes, nor forget, while obeying the call of appetite, the purpose for which it was implanted in him; and the mother will not neglect her children to practise the arts of coquetry when good sense and modesty secure her husband’s friendship.

But until men pay attention to the duty of a father, it is useless to expect women to spend in the nursery the time that they, “wise in their generation,” choose to spend at their mirrors. For this exercise of cunning is only a natural instinct that enables them to obtain indirectly a little of the power in which they are unjustly denied a share; and if women are not permitted to enjoy legitimate rights, they will make both men and themselves vicious in order to obtain illicit privileges.

I wish, sir, to set some inquiries of this kind in motion in France; and should they end by confirming my principles, then when your constitution is revised, the rights of woman may be respected — if it is fully proved that reason calls for this respect and loudly demands JUSTICE for one half of the human race.
I am, sir,
Yours respectfully,
M. W.
